title: Applied ML Eval Harness, Prompt Sets & Regression Triage Playbook
author: Asha Patel
content:
Overview

This playbook describes the end-to-end Applied ML evaluation process used at Redwood Inference: how the eval-harness is integrated with prompt sets and benchmarks, the model onboarding checklist, quality guardrails, quantization profile considerations, and an operational regression triage procedure. The intended audience is ML engineers, SREs working on serving, and product owners responsible for model quality and rollout.

Goals
- Provide a single reference that links eval harness workflows, benchmark construction, and triage steps.
- Ensure regressions are detected early and have a clear remediation path.
- Standardize quantization checks that preserve customer-facing quality.

Contents
1) Eval Harness integration
2) Prompt sets & benchmark design
3) Model onboarding checklist (quality + perf)
4) Quality guardrails and alert thresholds
5) Quantization profile validation
6) Regression triage playbook (operational steps)

1) Eval Harness integration

Intro
The eval-harness is the canonical runner for deterministic and stochastic evaluations across: text generation, chat flows, embedding similarity, and reranking tasks. It supports YAML configs, artifacts storage in S3, and automatic metrics ingestion into the Eval DB.

Key components
- Runner: python package (redwood_eval) used by CI and ad-hoc jobs.
- Configs: repo-level YAML under eval-configs/ describing model, dataset, seeds, sampling settings.
- Output: metrics.json + per-example outputs + artifact manifest (S3 path).
- Integration: GitHub Actions pipeline triggers + scheduled nightly jobs against production model variants.

Example CLI
- Run a smoke eval locally: python -m redwood_eval.run --config eval-configs/smoke-generation.yaml --output-dir ./out
- Run embedding benchmark: python -m redwood_eval.run --config eval-configs/embedding-bench-1.yaml --mode embedding

Config snippet (example YAML described in-line)
- model: "redwood-open-7b-v2"
- dataset: "prompt-sets/core-conversational-v1"
- seeds: [42, 123]
- sampling: {temperature: 0.7, top_p: 0.95}
- metrics: [bertscore, sacrebleu, exact_match, rouge_l]

2) Prompt sets & benchmark design

Principles
- Representative: benchmark prompts must mirror production distribution (routes, lengths, user intents).
- Targeted: include targeted prompt slices for known failure modes (e.g., math, code, hallucination).
- Deterministic vs stochastic: have both deterministic test cases (exact match) and probabilistic metrics (BERTScore, embedding cosine).

Structure of a prompt set (recommended)
- Metadata: id, short_description, author, created_at, tags.
- Cases: list of (prompt, expected_behavior, evaluation_metric, tolerance).
- Versions: maintain semantic versioning (v1.0.0) and changelog.

Example prompt-slice table (CSV-style)
| slice_id | n_examples | primary_metric | trigger_threshold | owner | notes |
| math-short | 150 | exact_match_rate | 85% | @noah.kim | small numeric reasoning problems |
| hallucination-news | 200 | factual_consistency | 95% | @sofia.m | entity hallucination on named entities |

Benchmarking cadence
- Nightly: smoke coverage of top 5 routes.
- Weekly: full regression suite (all prompt sets).
- Pre-release: full benchmark + human eval on top 1k examples before canary.

Storage and provenance
- All prompt sets live in git under eval-prompt-sets/. Changes require PR and a short changelog entry.
- Benchmarks and outputs are stored in S3: s3://redwood-eval-artifacts/{run_id}/
- Each run must record model git commit, container image, and quantization profile id.

3) Model onboarding checklist (quality + perf)

Before a model version is considered for production/Dedicated pools, complete the checklist below. Ownership: model-onboarding (engineering) with reviewer from applied-ml.

Mandatory checks
1. Unit tests: model loading and inference smoke (latency < SLO for dev instance).
2. Eval suite: run nightly + full benchmark. Metrics: all primary metrics must be within guardrail thresholds (see section 4).
3. Latency benchmarking: p50/p95/p99 measured with representative tokens and batch sizes. Document GPU type (A100/H100), kernel configuration, and batch sizes.
4. Cost estimate: tokens/sec and projected RU cost compared to baseline model.
5. Quantization compatibility: baseline 8-bit and 4-bit eval runs (if supported).
6. Security scan: model artifacts scanned and provenance recorded.
7. Human review: sample of 500 outputs across key slices reviewed by QA.

Onboarding docs to include (in PR)
- Model spec: architecture, tokenizer, expected sequence length.
- Eval report: full metrics.json and highlighted failures.
- Perf report: benchmarking CSV, flame graphs (if applicable).
- Rollout plan: canary percentages, rollback criteria, monitoring dashboard links.

4) Quality guardrails and alert thresholds

Alerting principles
- Alerts should be actionable and mapped to owners. Avoid noisy per-example alerts; aggregate by metric and slice.
- Use both absolute thresholds and relative change alarms (delta from baseline).

Primary metrics and thresholds
- Generation fluency (BERTScore F1): must not drop by >2.0 points relative to baseline for core routes.
- Exact match / pass@1 (deterministic tests): drop >3% absolute triggers P1.
- Embedding cosine on canonical pairs: drop >0.02 average triggers investigation.
- Latency: p95 increase >25% relative to baseline triggers perf triage.
- Erroneous hallucination rate (labeled slices): increase >2% absolute triggers P1.

Example monitoring rule (Prometheus/Alertmanager)
- name: eval_regression_p1
- expr: (bertscore_core_routes_baseline - bertsore_core_routes_current) > 2.0
- severity: P1
- owner: applied-ml

5) Quantization profile validation

Profile types
- fp16 (baseline)
- int8 dynamic (recommended for 7B-13B models if kernels supported)
- nf4 / 4-bit GPTQ profiles for low-memory deployments

Validation checklist
1. Functional parity: run exact-match deterministic suite (sanity) and measure delta on primary metrics.
   - Allowable deltas: BERTScore delta <= 1.0, exact-match delta <= 2% absolute for non-critical slices.
2. Stability: ensure per-example logits-based nearest neighbors and embedding cosine do not systematically shift (mean shift < 0.01).
3. Performance: measure token/sec and GPU memory. Document changes in p50/p95 latencies.
4. Edge-case stress tests: long-context (>2048 tokens), caching behavior, and KV-cache correctness.

Quantization artifact tagging
- Each quantized artifact must include metadata fields (as part of artifact manifest): quant_profile_id, quant_tool_version, rng_seed, validation_run_id.

6) Regression triage playbook (operational steps)

Scope
This section defines how to respond when an automated eval-run flags a regression (threshold breach) or when monitoring surfaces a quality/perf regression in production.

Initial triage (first 30 minutes)
1. Acknowledge: assigned owner from the alert. Post to #applied-ml-alerts with run_id and top-level metrics.
2. Confirm: re-run the failing eval job locally/CI with the same run_id and model artifact. Use: python -m redwood_eval.run --run-id <run_id> --recompute
3. Classify: is this a metric drift (gradual) or a step-change (deploy/quantization/infra)? Check recent deploys and quant_profile changes over the last 24 hours.

If metric regression confirmed (30-90 minutes)
- Collect artifacts: metrics.json, per-example diffs (baseline vs current), and sample outputs for high-impact slices.
- Check perf: p95 latency metrics and GPU utilization at the time of the run.
- Quick rollback: if regression coincides with a model rollout and cannot be triaged quickly, trigger the rollout rollback policy (see rollout plan).

Root cause steps (90 minutes–6 hours)
1. Narrow by slice: run per-slice delta analysis and aggregate by tag (e.g., math, security, named-entities).
2. Test quantization impact: re-run eval with fp16 artifact (if available) to isolate quantization vs model change.
3. Reproduce with deterministic seeds and deterministic decoding (greedy) to find systematic differences.
4. Investigate infra/kernel changes: consult kernel-and-scheduling release notes and infra change logs.

Human review & severity classification
- P1: customer-facing outage or large quality regression on top routes (requires incident response and a rollback within SLA).
- P2: significant regression on non-core slices that needs small-fix or model patch.
- P3: minor degradations tracked as backlog items.

Communication and postmortem
- If P1/P2: create an incident ticket, assign SRE and ML owners, and follow the oncall-and-incident-response process.
- Postmortem (template): timeline, detection method, root cause, mitigation steps, corrective actions (test additions, guardrail changes), and owners.

Preventative measures and continuous improvement
- Expand prompt sets when new failure modes are found and link these to automated tests (regression watchlists).
- Add human-in-the-loop checks for sensitive categories (legal, medical, finance).
- Tune alert thresholds to balance sensitivity vs noise; record any threshold changes in the alert changelog.

Appendix A: Quick commands and paths
- Eval runner: git repo: git@github.com:redwood-inference/eval-harness.git
- Run locally: python -m redwood_eval.run --config eval-configs/<config>.yaml
- Artifact S3: s3://redwood-eval-artifacts/{run_id}/metrics.json
- Prompt sets path: eval-prompt-sets/<slice_name>/README.md

Appendix C: Example alert runbook snippet
1. Alert fires: eval_regression_p1
2. Pager duty: notify applied-ml rotation
3. Triage channel: #applied-ml-alerts with run_id and S3 artifact link
4. Immediate action: if regression > configured rollback threshold, pause rollout and rollback to last known-good model.
